title: Chiral thermal fluctuations and enhanced refrigeration in a nonreciprocal nanomechanical system
authors: Jesse J. Slim, Javier del Pino, Sander A. Mann, Ewold Verhagen
abstract: Understanding how the breaking of reciprocity influences thermal flows and microscopic thermodynamic processes such as refrigeration and energy conversion is of broad current interest. We report experimental measurements of thermal flows and refrigeration in nanomechanical resonator networks in which nonreciprocity is controlled through an optically-induced synthetic magnetic flux. Time-modulated optomechanical interactions allow controlled coupling, gauge fields, and refrigeration processes through nanomechanical frequency conversion. We quantify nonequilibrium heat flows between resonators coupled to dissipative baths of different occupation and image heat and effective temperature in networks through measuring correlations of fluctuations. Synthetic magnetism is shown to imprint chirality on thermal fluctuations in a loop of resonators, leading to pronounced chiral flows with different handedness in distinct frequency bands. We find that the heat flows in a non-equilibrium system are tuned by the synthetic magnetic flux, which redistributes energy in the thermal steady-state. Specifically, we illustrate how nonreciprocity enhances the refrigeration of a resonator in the strong coupling regime, reducing its temperature below the bound that applies to time-reversal symmetric networks. These results experimentally demonstrate the impact of nonreciprocity on thermodynamic machines, and provide new methods to characterize them at the microscopic level.
summary: The authors experimentally demonstrate that controlling nonreciprocity in a nanomechanical resonator network using synthetic magnetism allows for the creation of chiral thermal currents. This chirality enhances refrigeration effects, enabling the system to cool below theoretical bounds applicable when time-reversal symmetry is preserved. The work provides a powerful platform for studying directed energy transport at the nanoscale.
main_problem: The study investigates how breaking time-reversal symmetry (nonreciprocity) influences microscopic thermodynamic processes like heat flow and refrigeration in nanoscale systems.
main_result: Nonreciprocity, controlled by a synthetic magnetic flux, imprints chirality on thermal fluctuations, leading to enhanced cooling below the limits set for time-reversal symmetric networks.
method: The research combines experimental measurements of thermal flows with theoretical analysis using correlation functions and spectral density calculations derived from coupled oscillator dynamics.
model_or_system: The system is a nanomechanical resonator network, specifically analyzed as a loop or dimer structure. Nonreciprocity is engineered via an optically-induced synthetic magnetic flux controlling the coupling Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Heat flow ($Q_{j	o k}$), effective temperature, chiral circulation of thermal fluctuations, and steady-state correlations $R_{jk}(	au)$.
important_parameters: Synthetic magnetic flux ($\Phi$), bath occupation imbalance ($\Delta n_{th}$), and coupling strengths ($J$).
main_assumptions: Baths are modeled as Markovian and independent; the analysis relies on gauge-invariant fluxes around closed loops.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, time-resolved correlation functions showing thermalization, and heat flow diagrams demonstrating chiral currents in response to flux bias.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical platform (nanomechanical network) to quantifying non-equilibrium energy transport using correlations. It first examines dimer dynamics, then extends to loop systems where chirality is quantified by the magnetic flux, culminating in the demonstration of enhanced refrigeration.
why_interesting: This work provides an experimental realization and quantitative measure of how engineered broken symmetries (nonreciprocity) can fundamentally alter fundamental thermodynamic limits, which has implications for quantum heat engines and energy conversion.
